opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a very natural analogy, because managing a team and training a model have a lot in common. You're trying to get a complex system to produce good behavior, and you have two basic tools: you can show people exactly what to do, or you can define what "good" looks like and let them find their own way there.

Supervised fine-tuning is like the first one. You give very detailed instructions: here's the task, here's how to do it, step by step, here's the expected output. The advantage is that it's efficient and predictable. If someone is new, or the task is well understood, this is the fastest way to get them productive. But the ceiling is the person giving the instructions. If I tell everyone exactly what to do, the team can at best be as good as my own judgment, and that's a pretty low ceiling for a frontier research organization.

Reinforcement learning is more like setting the reward. You tell people what outcome matters, why it matters, and how we'll know if we've succeeded, and then you give them room to explore. People might try things you'd never have thought of. Some will fail, but some will find much better solutions than anything you could have prescribed. In research, especially when you're working on problems nobody has solved yet, I think that's essential. You can't SFT your way to something genuinely new.

So my bias is toward more RL, but with a few caveats that also mirror the technical side.

First, the reward has to be well designed. If you define the wrong objective, people will optimize it very effectively and you'll get reward hacking: metrics go up but the real goal doesn't move. So a lot of a manager's job is actually thinking hard about what the right reward is and communicating it clearly, rather than micromanaging the actions.

Second, you need a good initialization. In model training, RL works much better on top of a strong pretrained model with some SFT. With people it's similar. You want to hire people with strong fundamentals and good taste, and you give some upfront alignment on culture, standards, and how we think about problems. After that you can rely much more on outcome-based feedback.

Third, the balance depends on the stage and on the person. For someone just joining, or for a task where we already know the right answer, more direct guidance makes sense. For experienced people working on open-ended problems, you mostly want to get out of the way and focus on giving good feedback.

And I'd add that the feedback loop matters a lot. RL only works if the signal comes back quickly and honestly. In a team, that means people need to see the results of what they did, and there needs to be an environment where you can say "this didn't work" without it being a big deal. If exploration is punished, people will just collapse to the safe, conservative policy, and you lose the whole benefit.

So, roughly: a little SFT to get the foundation and shared values right, then mostly RL with a carefully designed reward and fast, honest feedback. That's how I try to think about it, though I won't pretend I always get the balance right.

r001.rationale: It compares reinforcement learning to setting a reward by telling the team which outcomes matter and how success will be measured.

r002.rationale: It tentatively favors more reinforcement learning, concluding with a little SFT followed by mostly RL.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the analogy actually holds up pretty well, and it's something I've thought about a lot since Moonshot started growing.

Supervised fine-tuning is when you give someone very explicit demonstrations. Here is the problem, here is how to solve it, here is what good output looks like. For a new team member, or for a task where we already know the answer and just need it executed well, that's efficient. You don't want people rediscovering things we've already figured out. There's a lot of institutional knowledge in how we train models, how we run experiments, and transmitting that directly saves months.

But SFT has the same limitation in people that it has in models. If you only ever imitate, your ceiling is the ceiling of the demonstrations. You don't get anything beyond what's already in the data. And in AI research right now, the problems that matter most are ones where nobody has the demonstration. Nobody knows what the right architecture or the right data recipe is for the next step. So for those problems you need something closer to RL. You give people a clear reward signal, which for us is usually a well-defined metric or a very concrete goal, and you let them explore. They'll try things that fail, and that's fine. The exploration is the point.

The hard part is the reward design. If the reward is wrong, people optimize for the wrong thing, exactly like a model does. If you reward activity you get lots of experiments and no insight. If you reward papers you get papers. So a lot of my job is actually making sure the reward signal reflects what we care about, which is usually: did the model get better on something that matters to users.

In terms of balance, I think it shifts over time. Early on with a person, more SFT. As they build judgment, you reduce the demonstrations and let the reward signal do more of the work. And for the organization as a whole, I'd rather lean toward the RL side, because the thing I'm most afraid of is a team that executes very well on a plan that's already outdated. The frontier moves too fast for pure imitation.

One more thing. In models, good RL still needs a reasonable SFT base, otherwise exploration is just random. I think it's the same with teams. You need enough shared context and taste so that when people explore, they explore in sensible directions. So it's not really either-or. It's foundation first, then let the reward take over.

r001.rationale: It compares RL’s reward signal with a team’s well-defined metric or concrete goal, identifying team goals as the analogue of rewards.

r002.rationale: It says that for the organization as a whole, it would rather lean toward the RL side.

astra-6.text:
I think you need both. Supervised fine-tuning, as a management analogy, is showing people what good work looks like: giving examples, sharing your reasoning, and establishing some basic standards. That’s especially useful when someone is new, because you can’t expect them to discover everything through trial and error.

Reinforcement learning is more like giving people a clear objective, letting them choose how to approach it, and providing feedback on the results. That gives the team room to find approaches you wouldn’t have thought of yourself.

The balance depends on the person and the task. If the task is familiar and mistakes are costly, more guidance makes sense. If it’s research and nobody knows the answer, you need more freedom to explore. But the feedback matters a lot. If you reward only short-term results, people may avoid worthwhile risks. So I’d give clear examples where we have knowledge, and encourage experimentation where we don’t.

r001.rationale: The response describes giving a clear objective and feedback as part of the reinforcement-learning analogy, but does not clearly identify setting team objectives as analogous to providing rewards.

r002.rationale: It says the balance depends on the person and task, recommending guidance for familiar work and experimentation for uncertain work. It does not tentatively favor a balance weighted toward reinforcement learning overall.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the analogy is that supervised fine-tuning is showing people what good work looks like, while reinforcement learning is giving them a goal and letting them discover how to achieve it. You need both, but the balance depends on how much context the team has.

When someone is new, concrete examples and close feedback are very useful. If you only give them an outcome metric, they may spend a lot of time rediscovering things you already know. But as they develop judgment, you want to give them more autonomy. Otherwise, the team’s capabilities become limited by what the manager knows how to demonstrate.

The difficult part is defining the reward. If you reward something that is easy to measure but only loosely connected to what you actually want, people will optimize for that. So I would be explicit about the goal, provide examples where they help, and leave room for people to find a better approach than mine.

r001.rationale: The response describes reinforcement learning as giving the team a goal and later says to define the reward and be explicit about the goal, communicating team objectives as the reward analogue.

r002.rationale: The response says the balance depends on team context and recommends more autonomy as people gain judgment, but it does not state an overall preference for a balance weighted toward reinforcement learning.
